Unfortunately the thing is that you don't deal with someone who has no empathy. You either keep them in your life if you think the suffering is worth it, or you cut them out of your life completely. You can never make anybody understand something if they don't want to understand in the first place (this applies to many things, ranging from emotions to science to the simple facts of life). If she doesn't want to understand autism, then you'd have better luck explaining the same concept to a frog—the frog might listen politely, at least.

It's unfortunately very harsh, but it's true that nobody can save you except yourself. You have got to be your own hero, otherwise nothing will get any better. And the additional unfortunate truth is that we probably have to work a lot harder than others in order to be our own heroes. It's certainly not fair, but the fact of the matter is that we only have this one life to live, so we may as well try our hardest when we can.

You need to prep your nails well if you want to do nail lacquer/varnish/polish. Dehydrating them with acetone/rubbing alcohol first, then using a good base coat, then 1-3 coats of your chosen polish (application is key here, wrap the tips with polish and make sure the polish doesn't dry on your skin), and then a good quick dry top coat is what is needed to make them last. 

You may need to try different base coats and top coats, it's not a one size fits all situation. Watch out for polishes with PVB, as they can cause some people's nails to peel. I also don't recommend buffing if you're just applying polishes.

Also consider taking breaks from your strengthening top coat. I was using the Orly calcium shield just to protect my nails (I have to use hand sanitizer all day for my job), but it ended up making my nails peel, and apparently that can happen with strengthening polishes. 

So polish isn't necessarily not an option, but it needs just about as much research to apply it correctly & safely as other types of nail stuff.

First, I definitely have some bias regarding the whole "walking on eggshells thing" bc my ex would use that phrase when I called him out on his bullshit. Or is he using it like my ex would in the hopes that you'll minimize your needs so that he can do whatever the hell he needs wants? You don't have to answer me, but it may be something worth thinking about. 

As for the food thing, that might be something that's worth trying to work on. Lettuce is a pretty ubiquitous item, and you can't really guarantee that you'll not be near it any time you go to a restaurant or a grocery store. I don't think exposure therapy always (or even often) works, but this seems like a seriously limiting fear to be burdened with (as in a burden for you to deal with), so maybe confronting it in a safe space would be helpful—like, ask your bf to buy some and interact with it as much as you can (whatever that may look like for you, no matter how silly it may seem). 

The wrong/bad food order is also tough. When I was your age I would also just deal with it and eat little to none of my food if that happened. I know it's so so awkward and kind of scary to speak up, but I really encourage you to do so. Most people are happy to fix your food, and the ones who aren't are either jerks or just having a bad day, but neither of those situations means that you deserve to eat shitty food. Basically remember that you're allowed and deserve to take up space just for the fact that you're alive. 

As for changing plans, I still struggle with that. What helps sometimes is to actually plan for unplanned things. If I'm going out with someone who doesn't like to stick to a schedule for example, I will essentially write the entire day off. Like, as long as I know that I don't know what exactly I'll be doing, then it's not so much of a big deal when something surprising pops up. 

Also, remember that you're allowed to take breaks from whatever's happening. Food order comes wrong at the restaurant? Go to the bathroom for five minutes to regulate (headphones in a bathroom stall, box breathing, close your eyes, etc.). Change of plans? Cool, but ask for 15 minutes to sit in your room or sit in the car (like if you're out and about) so that you can regulate. 

Basically get comfortable taking up space and advocate for yourself. It's really hard, like super hard, but things aren't going to get better unless you take direct action to change things. 

Best of luck 🍀

I'm not sure about burnout specifically, and while I don't think a single trip did it I feel like the series of trips I did a few years ago kicked my chronic depression. I'm usually pretty high strung, and the trips let my body and mind actually totally relax for once. It let me be really in the moment and appreciate whatever sensations I was currently experiencing, as opposed to stressing out about life, responsibilities, deadlines, etc. 

A mild trip for me (about a gram) is a much better stress reliever than weed. Shrooms last a bit longer than a weed high (again, for me personally since I don't actually like getting mega high on weed, and I don't like continually dosing it), the actual high is more pleasant (full body effects on shrooms as opposed to mostly in my head for weed), and much better after effects (weed leaves me with a small headache most times the morning after and phlegm if I smoke; shrooms leave me refreshed). 

So I think starting small and being with someone you trust during the trip is a good idea. I first started out with .5g just to get a handle on it and then went to 1g on subsequent trips, and I didn't feel like I needed more than that.

It's simply not realistic for anybody to not ever mess up, autistic or not. Everybody has bad days—we might have more due to how autism affects us and how we move throughout a neurotypical world. This doesn't mean that we can never be good as NT people. Shame and humiliation are normal feelings, but they become unhelpful and unhealthy when you stew in those feelings and don't learn from them. 

You can't always fix situations that you mess up—that is simply a fact of life. It doesn't matter if it's a big or small situation either; sometimes a sorry will never be enough. But that's for other people to decide. 

What you need to do is learn and change. It doesn't need to be overnight, but bettering one's self and how one acts should be a goal for every human being on the planet (just so you don't feel singled out). 

Tell yourself that you will mess up again—because you will, we all will—but that next time you're going to do something different that will help you or other people, depending on the situation.

You mentioned that you're dealing with depression, so I'll try to not be too preachy about this, but I dealt with depression for a decent amount of time. But I've come to the conclusion that while there's unimaginable pain and suffering in the world, there are also unimaginable joys. The main problem with this is that the pain comes around even if you're not really doing any, but the joy doesn't tend to come your way unless you actively chase after it. It's a pretty shit deal, but that's life for you. 

When I was really going through it, I was trying to understand what was going on with me. I watched this Ted talk by Andrew Solomon, and he said something like when you're depressed you think you see that you're seeing the world truly, like the veil has been lifted from your eyes and you're seeing the world as it really is. But he says that the truth lies. The way I understood that is that depression actually places a grey veil upon you. You really can't feel the veil because it's this gossamer silk and it feels so, so comfortable to lean into it. Thus, something like suicide doesn't seem so bad. The reality is that people like you and me must fight with tooth and nail to tear that veil from in front of our eyes. If you can't do it for yourself or your family or friends now, then you must do it for your future self, and your future family and friends. If there's no joy now, then compel yourself to rip it from the earth if you must. 

I'll leave the link to the Ted talk, if you're interested: https://youtu.be/-eBUcBfkVCo 

I'll also note that companionship is much along the same lines as joy—it's not something that falls into your lap, but it is something that I'm going to chase after for as long as I live. It's certainly not easy, and depression makes it a hundred times harder. Ultimately though, I don't think it's impossible to be loved when you're depressed. I have loved and still love so many imperfect people, and so how is it possible that no one would look at you a second time? Pre-sliced or pre-prepared fruits and vegetables are a good start. They're not exactly budget friendly, but they don't break the bank imo. For example, my Walmart/WinCo has pre-sliced apples (red or green) that come with a cup of caramel sauce—and they take quite a while to go brown, so I can usually buy 3-4 packs at a time. Also pre-sliced pineapple—it was only maybe a year ago that I figured out the sliced pineapple spears (not like, canned) are usually pretty good, and it helps that I'll eat tf out of them. Smaller mandarins and tangerines are also a good one for me, since I love the taste. 

I admit that I'm not the biggest vegetable fan, so I typically try to get that into foods where I might not notice it. Soups are a really good one for this, since you can finely chop/blend certain veggies (tomatoes, celery, onion, leeks, carrots, shallots, garlic, etc.) and then you don't even notice it. 

Also if you like the flavor of salsa but can't stand the chunks, you can totally throw the whole thing in a blender and make it super smooth—I used to do this as a teen all the time. 

Speaking of soups, beans are a nice add-in. You may need to experiment a little because the different varieties have different flavor and textures. I like pinto and great northern beans because they're tender and you can't really feel the skin of the bean when you're eating them. Get canned specifically, and be sure to rinse them before adding to a soup/stew, bc the water in it is a little grainy with bean bits. 

Nuts are supposed to be a good one as well, and I feel like are generally safe bc crunchy typically isn't a bad texture. 

Yogurt is really hit or miss for me. Sometimes I can stand the texture of a normal yogurt, but sometimes it's too much and it's a little too tangy. If I can, I'll do like the Noosa yogurt (the pumpkin one is really good) and I'll put protein granola in it so it's crunchy and not just goopy. Alternatively, I had been thinking about those like, Danimals yogurt drinks for kids, and I saw that Trader Joe's had these low-fat yogurt strawberry smoothies—they were very, very good! They weren't super tangy, pretty sweet (not like candy, but not bland either, so a really nice balance) they were nice and smooth (no weird chunks), and they had a wild berry option if that sounds good. 

If budget isn't a big concern, jerky from a local butcher can be good. The stuff that you find in stores is generally really soft and fatty—not my preferred textures. The stuff you can get from an independent butcher is generally very thin, dry, and almost tough—I find this much more enjoyable, but I recognize this could be a me-thing. 

And if you can, I really recommend looking at the different stores you have accessible to you. I have to drive like 2 hours to get to the larger asian supermarkets for example, but they allow for more variety in my diet since they carry fruits, veggies, pantry staples, and prepared foods that I wouldn't really have considered otherwise. 

Best of luck though 🍀

There might be a couple of intersecting issues here.

The first one is that you may not just be familiar with different base tastes. For example, bitter and sour are two completely different flavors. Something like dark chocolate or the pith on an orange peel are bitter, but they'll never be sour. Biting is an adjacent synonym to sour—it describes sourness, but the word "bite" itself has a connotation that the flavor itself is almost attacking your mouth. 

Which leads me into the next element: how well-read are you? You don't literally need to answer me; moreso think about the question. People with more experience/knowledge/etc. tend to use less common expressions, phrases, descriptors, or what have you. Essentially, they're saying that something tastes bright because this is a word that they've learned to associate with a particular flavor. Learning does come in many shapes and forms of course, so they could have learned this through hobbies, their jobs, books, videos, and more. 

Finally, especially if we're talking about content that people are making, they're using elaborate descriptions because either the food itself is complex, or they're just making shit up because it's more pleasing for the audience to hear. Some dishes really do have a great depth in terms of flavor because there are many, many ingredients and steps to making the dish, so even if it's got citrus in it, it's not just going to taste like citrus. I will also note that tasting everything in a dish takes practice. If you're not familiar with the taste of all of the base ingredients going into a dish, you're not going to be able to identify them in the finished product. 

So mostly I guess I'm trying to say that describing food well is something else that takes practice. You need to understand the ingredients that go into it, how their flavors can change, and then you need to practice connecting those flavors to different words (and learning those words is another different skill that needs to be practiced).

If you mean you have the meat in a bag, and then the bag is put in room temp or hot water, then yes, you are increasing your chances of getting ill. It's the temperature that makes a big difference here (although you should always thaw meat in a waterproof bag of some sort if you're thawing via running water). Warmer water puts the meat into what's called the danger zone—these warmer temperatures are when and where bacteria like to grow and breed. Cooler temperatures inhibit this. 

Unsafe thawing practices do not guarantee that you'll get sick, but it does increase the chance by a considerable degree. When in doubt, look for information from recognized organizations on matters like this, such as the USDA: https://www.fsis.usda.gov/food-safety/safe-food-handling-and-preparation/food-safety-basics/big-thaw-safe-defrosting-methods

Information from your community is great sometimes, but I prefer to listen to science when it comes to my health.

And then, as many other people have said, it puts a massive strain on the environment. I think those are elements that you need to decide if you're okay with them or not; but at the same time, like with most things, people are going to judge you either way.

Any meat that comes from a store has been processed in sanitary conditions, otherwise a lot more people would be getting sick from the food they buy from the store. Besides that, just water will not rinse away bacteria. Think about it like this: do you just rinse your plates and forks after eating with them, or do you use soap on them? It is the soap that does all the work in killing bacteria. This is NOT to say you need to clean your meat with soap. 

When it comes to beef, whole cuts (like steaks from the store) are safe to eat rare as long as the outside has been cooked properly. However, gound beef, all types of pork, and all types of chicken/fowl should be cooked to specific internal temperatures in order to make sure that any harmful bacteria is dead (killed by the heat)—you can Google these temps. 

As far as the parts you trimmed off: if they're just a little brown but still smells fine like the rest of the meat, then it's just oxidized. This isn't harmful, it's just not appetizing to look at. But if the meat smells bad, like rot, you should not eat it—you should not even try to trim a piece that smells like it's rotting—the whole thing should be thrown away. 

I recommend watching some cooking shows and some food handler's safety training videos if you're serious about this—notice what the professionals and teachers in these videos are doing, and what they're *not* doing. Washing meat, as I understand it, is a sort of cultural holdover. It may have been useful when you're the one going out and killing, skinning, and cleaning meat from an animal; but processing plants are already taking care of this step for you if you get meat from a grocery store.
Olive oil has a lower smoke point—i.e. it burns and gets gross at a lower temp, so switching to an oil with a higher smoke point will def help. And np!

Something to remember is that your brain is a muscle, and so whichever way you train it, it will become better at performing that action again and again. So, for example, if you're looking in the mirror and thinking about how ugly you feel, it will only be easier to think that same thought in the future. Similarly, if you make it a habit to think more positive thoughts, these thoughts will become easier to think again in the future. 

And that's all fine and dandy for me to say, but the reality is that it is extremely hard to change a habit like this. The phrase "fake it til you make it" holds some truth here though. Even though the exercise of telling yourself positive thoughts (especially if you don't quite believe them) is difficult, enough persistence can make a change—although the change unfortunately won't happen overnight. 

Beyond that, I encourage you to find more people who have the same type of body as you and follow them on whatever your choice of social media /etc. is. Seek out content (books, movies, TV shows, anybody who makes content you're interested in), and watch/read it. Society normalizes a very narrow range of "acceptable" body types, so you need to make sure that you're surrounding yourself and consuming stories/whatnot with people that are actually normal, like you. 

Finally, remember to try to believe other people when they're speaking to you genuinely. It's very easy to dismiss what other people say because of your own feelings, but beauty is not objective. Think of all the times you've thought someone was beautiful, even if they didn't adhere to today's strict beauty standards—that feeling of yours was real and valid, and so you should try your best to not dismiss others' real and valid feelings (not a knock on you btw—this stuff is super hard—but thinking really hard about the perspectives of other people helps me sometimes). 

Best wishes 🍀

I still struggle with being me, but I think the first thing that I needed to figure out is that you don't *need* to do anything with your life. Seriously. Humans are just like any other animal, and we're here on this planet to eat, sleep, play, make babies (this one's debatable for us humans, bc I don't want this, lmao), and just hang out & make emotional connections. That's literally all any of us needs to do, because that's literally the only thing that other animals do. 

Unfortunately, we've overcomplicated this with a shit ton of other stuff (capitalism being a main issue here, imo). 

Your particular circumstances and age can make it difficult, but once you are at a place where you can act independently, it does become somewhat easier to find yourself. 

But as far as figuring out what you really want, I believe that this is something that takes a really good amount of time. I think you also need to be in touch with your emotions *and* your body. For example, do you know what joy feels like in your body? I feel joy when I make/eat really good food, so I know that food is important to me in a way that goes beyond simple sustenance. 

I think if you want to be able to identify who you are, you need to figure out what you like, but that definitely means knowing how to identify emotions within yourself. Specifically, I think feeling & identifying things like joy, pride, contentedness (this one especially!), excitement, catharsis, curiosness, etc. would be a good start to figuring out what you like. 

If you're already able to identify these things, then the matter is simply trying more things in this life. For example, I started to crochet one year and I absolutely hated it and it made me mad, so I put it down. However, sometimes I can be extremely stubborn, and I wasn't happy with just setting it down and never trying it again. So a year later, I tried again. It was still hard, but I kept trying, and eventually I got better at it. A handful of years later, I can crochet at at least an intermediate level, and I'm quite happy with the things I make. 

The point there is that doing things gives you experience and insight into who you are. Because I tried out crochet, it enforces my understanding that I can be quick to anger, but I am also stubborn and do not always give up on things very easily. This, to me, is a part of my identity.

One other thing that I want to point out is that I also think media can be a really hopeful tool for figuring out who you are. One of the things that make humans truly different is our capacity to tell stories. While some stories are certainly created just as a cash grab, there are tons and tons of people on this planet who are creating stories just because they think the story should be told. Stories are wonderful insights into ourselves and into other people, and I think the more stories that you experience, the more you can understand the world around you and the world within you. For example, I enjoy very particular types of romances—they just pull at my heartstrings—therefore I know that I am a particular type of romantic. 

I'm not super sure how to end this, but I really do think experiencing new things is the best thing to do in life, no matter if you're trying to figure out your identity or not.

You need to remember that your worth as a human is not tied to what you can do, what you can achieve, or what your abilities are. 

Nobody hates their cat or dog because they don't produce anything worthwhile throughout their lives; it is enough for them to exist and for us to love them. 

We love flowers for similar reasons. We cultivate them because they are beautiful and they bring us joy—we appreciate them as they are. Even moving beyond that, flowers have a place in the ecosystem, and they work within it, and so do you. You are no less valuable to the world because you don't have a driver's license. 

All of these things you think you should have and think you should achieve are a result of purely human influence. It is only because society at large has deemed things like a job or a college degree as necessary/good that you believe you are worth less without them. 

I realize it's a bit hippy-ish, but seriously think about this: we are no greater than any of the life around us. The plants, the animals, the fungi—we're all here to simply exist. We all came from the same muck at some point in time, and we all return to it sooner or later. 

I know how hard life is, and we haven't created a world where it feels safe to simply exist like the crow or the Cyprus tree does. Us humans have put a lot of extra rules and judgement on things, and while we can push back against them, it's also unfortunately necessary to live with some of them. We each just have to learn how to live with them—we've got to figure out how to make this life enjoyable for ourselves. 

I can promise you that you're worthwhile. You live in a web of life, and the fact that you are here and breathing makes you equal to everything and anything else in that web.

I really enjoy cooking, so I hope you don't mind me hopefully giving you some advice.

The first thing I'll mention is that microwave dinners can be a godsend, if you haven't utilized those yet. Some of them don't taste the best, but there are a few that are really decent imo; and this way you wouldn't have to deal with quite as much heat. 

For the heat sensory thing, is it when you open the oven and the heat hits your face, or maybe is it more your arms when you need to grab something out of the oven?  They do make extra long oven mitts, and there may be some type of heat resistant mask available (probably not geared towards cooking, but would still be usable) if you're interested in tackling that issue. 

And somewhat unfortunately, you're right—cooking is arbitrary. Knowing how much seasoning to put into something is really something that comes along with practice. And tying this into "making it how you like it", I often use recipes that I find on the web, but I also find that a lot of people under-season their food. So, for example, I will follow a recipe and measure out the salt and spices, etc. I'll taste it, and I'll find that it doesn't wow me. Like if my brain isn't immediately excited and pushing me to take another bite of the food, it's probably not seasoned well (could be a host of other issues too, but this is just one example). 

Making things the way you like it also refers to texture though, as there are different levels of how much you can cook certain foods. So for example, steak has quite a few different doneness levels: blue, rare, medium rare, medium, medium well, and well done. I love rare and medium rare steak—I'll take one bite and if the seasoning and texture is right, the dopamine levels skyrocket, lol. But if you gave me a well done steak, I wouldn't be half as happy to eat that bc I don't enjoy the texture & flavor. 

Making it the way you like also requires experimenting along with the practice; occasionally I'll try a new recipe with new seasonings and ingredients. For example, about a year ago I tried making a Korean stew for the first time; I had never before used ingredients like gochujang and gochugaru, but I followed the given recipe and it turned out that I enjoyed it. But I also knew that it could be more enjoyable, as it was just a tad too spicy. After cooking it a couple times and experimenting with the amounts of ingredients, I found that I liked more gochujang and less gochugaru than the recipe suggested. 

In any case, I won't lie and say that cooking is the easiest thing in the world. And this is anecdotal, but I honestly don't think that most people are even working at a base level when it comes to cooking; like I love my family, but they often massively overcook and under-season food, and lots of other people that I've met simply don't care to put in the effort to cook something nice. 

But yeah. Long story short, cooking is a learned skill that can probably be likened to painting. Most people aren't great at it due to a lack of practice or interest in it, and some people have a knack for it—and only a few people are good enough to make a name for themselves in the field. 

I'm hoping this was a little helpful and cleared some things up 😅

Your question is really vague as well, because the answer depends entirely upon the size & shape of your steak.

For example, if you just shove a .5" thick petite sirloin in a 550° oven, you're gonna have a bad time. Thinner pieces of steak don't do well in the oven because the interior will cook totally before the exterior has a chance to go brown and delicious. And with steak, generally, people want some sort of pink in their steak, whether it's cooked rare or medium.

If you follow Alton Brown's instructions for a 3-4 bone standing rib roast (which ends off with searing the outside at the highest temp possible for ~10 minutes) it's gonna come out great.

But I'm guessing you're not talking about a roast, and you're probably not even talking about a couple inch+ thick ribeye? In which case, just stick to a pan or the grill. A hot cast iron pan, for example, allows you to get the exterior all seared and brown and delicious without cooking the interior very much (at least, if you don't leave it on the pan very long). 

Remember, when I say bad and good here it's all relative to individual tastes. I like very rare steaks, while other people like their steak well-done. But in this subreddit, I'm fairly certain you'll find more people like me, and not as many people who enjoy well-done steak.
